screens.title: Monitoring, Logging, and Troubleshooting OpenShift Clusters
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we focus on the operational tools you need to keep an OpenShift cluster healthy. You will learn how OpenShift integrates Prometheus and Grafana for metrics and alerting, how the EFK stack centralizes application and platform logs, and how to use oc commands to diagnose and resolve common failures. We will ground each concept with short examples: exposing application metrics for Prometheus, reading container logs with oc logs, and running oc debug for node-level troubleshooting. You will also see how Fluentd collects logs and forwards them to Elasticsearch for analysis in Kibana. As an architect, your role is to combine proactive monitoring, clear alert rules, and centralized logging so incidents are detected early and investigated quickly. Throughout the lesson I will point out common mistakes, like jumping to node debugging before checking application logs or ignoring alerts from Alertmanager. By the end you will be able to read monitoring dashboards, search logs, and follow a step-by-step troubleshooting workflow that leads from symptom to root cause.

screens.title: Prometheus and Grafana — Roles and relationships
screens.narratorSegment: Prometheus and Grafana serve complementary roles. Prometheus is a time-series metrics store and alerting engine: it scrapes endpoints, stores samples, and evaluates alerting rules. Grafana connects to Prometheus to visualize that data and turn metrics into dashboards you can use during an incident or capacity exercise. Concretely, metrics like node C P U, pod restart counts, or custom application counters are recorded as time series in Prometheus and made visible in Grafana dashboards. A common example is C P U saturation on a node: Prometheus records rising C P U usage, Alertmanager triggers an alert, and Grafana shows the trend so you can correlate spikes with deployments or scheduled jobs. A typical misconception is to treat Grafana as the data source — Grafana only queries stored metrics; it does not collect them. Another common error is relying solely on dashboards without alerting. Dashboards are great for exploration, but alerting ensures you get notified when thresholds cross. Takeaway: think of Prometheus as the collector and rule evaluator, and Grafana as the interpreter and visual surface that helps you understand the numbers.

keyIdea.title: Collector vs. visualizer
keyIdea.text: Prometheus collects and stores metrics and evaluates alerts; Grafana visualizes them for human understanding and troubleshooting.

content.html:
Core Concept › Prometheus & Grafana
Prometheus: metrics and alerts
A pull-based time-series system that scrapes exporters and evaluates alerting rules.
  • Collects node and container metrics via exporters like kube-state-metrics and cAdvisor.
  • Stores sampled data as time series for trend analysis and alerting.
  • Integrates with Alertmanager to route alerts to responders.
Common misconception

Grafana is not a collector. If metrics are missing, check Prometheus scrape targets, not Grafana settings.

Grafana: dashboards and exploration
A visualization platform that queries Prometheus to render dashboards and panels for troubleshooting.
Example: node CPU trend and pod restart overlay help find correlation between deployments and CPU spikes.
Key takeaway

Use Prometheus for data and rules, Grafana to interpret results and guide remediation.

screens.title: Prometheus scrape targets and exporters
screens.narratorSegment: Prometheus gathers metrics by scraping targets that expose an HTTP endpoint in a Prometheus-compatible format. OpenShift deploys several exporters that turn internal state into scraped metrics. kube-state-metrics exposes object-level data about pods, deployments, and services. node-exporter gathers host-level metrics such as C P U, memory, disk, and network statistics. cAdvisor reports container-level resource usage. Applications can also expose custom metrics and be annotated so Prometheus will scrape them. A practical example is annotating a service so Prometheus picks up a /metrics endpoint; this is often the simplest way to make application counters available. A common mistake is not exposing metrics on a stable port or forgetting the scrape annotation. Another pitfall is overwhelming Prometheus with very high-cardinality labels from application metrics. The process to ensure reliable metric collection is: verify exporter pods are healthy, confirm scrape targets in Prometheus, and test an application endpoint. Doing this prevents missing data and reduces false alerts in Alertmanager. Prometheus scrape targets and exporters means exporters and annotated services are the source of truth for prometheus metrics; verify targets and endpoints when data is missing.. In practical terms, how kube-state-metrics, node-exporter, and cadvisor feed prometheus. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Scrape, expose, verify

content.html:
Process Flow › Exporter pipeline
Exporter roles
Each exporter converts cluster or host state into metrics Prometheus can scrape.
kube-state-metrics — object state for pods, deployments, services.
node-exporter — host-level CPU, memory, disk, network.
cAdvisor — container resource usage and live stats.
Checklist:
  • Are exporter pods running?
  • Does Prometheus list the expected scrape targets?
  • Does the app expose /metrics and use stable labels?
Common pitfall
High-cardinality labels from application metrics can overload Prometheus storage or cause slow queries — prefer stable, low-cardinality labels.
Example

Annotate a Service with prometheus.io/scrape=true to expose an application endpoint for scraping by Prometheus.

screens.title: Exposing application metrics in OpenShift
screens.narratorSegment: OpenShift discovers application metrics either through service discovery or explicit annotations. The recommended pattern is to annotate the Service or Pod so Prometheus will scrape a /metrics endpoint. For example, annotating a Service with prometheus. io/scrape set to true and prometheus. io/port to the correct port tells Prometheus to include that endpoint. After applying the annotation, you can verify the target in the Prometheus web UI or by checking Prometheus config in OpenShift. A practical trap is forgetting to expose the endpoint inside the container or using an ephemeral port that changes between restarts. If you don’t see metrics, check the Service and Pod labels, confirm the container serves metrics on the annotated port, and inspect Prometheus scrape targets. Misunderstanding here leads to gaps in visibility rather than broken collectors. Takeaway: a stable metrics endpoint with correct annotations ensures your application metrics are reliably collected and available for dashboards and alerting. Exposing application metrics in OpenShift means use stable annotations for prometheus scraping and validate targets to ensure application metrics appear in grafana dashboards.. In practical terms, annotate services and validate prometheus scrapes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Service annotation pattern
Example Service annotation
Apply an annotation so Prometheus scrapes the application endpoint.
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: myapp
  annotations:
    prometheus.io/scrape: "true"
    prometheus.io/port: "8080"
spec:
  selector:
    app: myapp
  ports:
  - name: http
    port: 8080
    targetPort: 8080
Notes: ensure the container serves /metrics on the annotated port and labels match the Service selector.
Verification steps
  1. Confirm Service and Pod labels match.
  2. Check Prometheus targets for the new endpoint.
  3. Open Grafana and query the metric name to validate presence.
Pitfall

If metrics are missing, confirm the container is actually listening and not blocked by network policies.

screens.title: EFK Stack — Fluentd, Elasticsearch, Kibana
screens.narratorSegment: OpenShift's integrated logging follows the EFK pattern: Fluentd collects logs, Elasticsearch stores and indexes them, and Kibana provides a user interface for searching and visualizing logs. Fluentd runs as a DaemonSet so each node forwards container stdout/stderr, system logs, and audit logs to Elasticsearch. Elasticsearch indexes logs to make searches fast and supports aggregations for analysis. Kibana sits on top and gives you the ability to query by labels, view recent events, and build visualizations that correlate with metric alerts. A practical example: when a pod restarts repeatedly, searching Kibana for that pod name and time range often reveals stack traces or exit messages that indicate a configuration or application bug. A common mistake is not sizing or managing log retention, which can cause Elasticsearch storage exhaustion. The ClusterLogging operator controls deployment; enabling it ensures Fluentd is configured cluster-wide. Takeaway: centralized logs are essential for root cause analysis and compliance, but they require operational care — index, retention, and storage must be planned. EFK Stack — Fluentd, Elasticsearch, Kibana means efk provides a searchable, centralized store of cluster and application logs that accelerates troubleshooting and supports audits.. In practical terms, how openshift centralizes logs for troubleshooting and audit. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept › EFK Stack
Fluentd — collector and forwarder
DaemonSet on each node collecting container logs, system logs, and audit trails and forwarding them to Elasticsearch.
Fluentd ensures logs are normalized and labeled so they are searchable in Kibana.
Elasticsearch + Kibana
Elasticsearch stores, indexes, and enables fast search and aggregations. Kibana provides the query and visualization surface.
Operational note

Plan index lifecycle and retention to avoid running out of storage in Elasticsearch; prune or archive old indices as needed.

screens.title: Fluentd as a DaemonSet and log flow
screens.narratorSegment: Fluentd is deployed as a DaemonSet so every node runs a collector that tails container logs and system journals. This node-local approach reduces cross-node log traffic and ensures logs are collected even if a pod is short-lived. Fluentd enriches logs with metadata such as namespace, pod name, and container name before forwarding them to Elasticsearch. In practice, when a pod crashes, Fluentd forwards the container output to Elasticsearch where you can search it in Kibana. A misconception is that logs are lost if a pod is short-lived; because Fluentd tails the node log files, it typically captures short-lived container output as long as Fluentd is running. Another operational concern is network reliability between Fluentd and Elasticsearch; use buffering and retries in Fluentd configuration to avoid data loss under transient network issues. Key takeaway: node-local Fluentd ensures consistent log ingestion, but the end-to-end pipeline requires attention to indexing, retention, and buffer settings. Fluentd as a DaemonSet and log flow means fluentd running on each node captures container and system logs reliably and forwards them to elasticsearch for indexing and search.. In practical terms, node-local collection and forwarding architecture. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Architecture › Fluentd flow
Log flow
Container stdout/stderr and node journals → Fluentd (DaemonSet) → Elasticsearch indices → Kibana search and dashboards.
Node-local Fluentd tails node logs and enriches them with metadata.
Fluentd forwards to Elasticsearch; indices make queries fast and support aggregations.
Kibana provides search, filters, and visualizations for incident investigation.
Operational considerations
  • Configure Fluentd buffering and retry to handle Elasticsearch outages.
  • Plan index lifecycle and retention to control storage use.
  • Monitor Fluentd and Elasticsearch health via Prometheus metrics and dashboards.

screens.title: Troubleshooting pods: common states and responses
screens.narratorSegment: Pod failures present with a small set of familiar symptoms. CrashLoopBackOff often means the container process exits repeatedly; the first diagnostic steps are oc describe pod to see events and oc logs to view the application output. For ImagePullBackOff, oc describe will show image pull errors — check ImageStream and registry credentials. Pending pods often indicate scheduling constraints like insufficient resources, node selectors, taints, or unresolved PVCs; oc describe pod will show scheduler messages pointing to the cause. Evicted pods usually result from node pressure, such as disk or memory exhaustion; check node status and events. A common mistake is to immediately SSH into nodes and change host settings before exhausting oc describe and oc logs; that wastes time and can introduce risk. Concrete example: a CrashLoopBackOff pod that prints "Simulating a crash" in its logs indicates the application command is exiting and requires changing the container command or image. Takeaway: start with oc describe and oc logs, interpret the events, and escalate to node-level debugging only after confirming the issue is host-related. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Pod states
Common pod conditions
  • CrashLoopBackOff: application exits repeatedly — check oc logs and the container command.
  • ImagePullBackOff: registry or ImageStream errors — verify image name and access.
  • Pending: scheduling constraints, taints, or PVC binding issues.
  • Evicted: node resource pressure; inspect node conditions.
Example commands
oc describe pod <pod-name> -n <project>
oc logs <pod-name> -n <project>
oc exec <pod-name> -- /bin/sh -c 'env && ps aux'
Start here to gather events and application output before performing host-level changes.

screens.title: Node and networking issues — Symptoms and checks
screens.narratorSegment: Node and networking issues can look similar from a pod's perspective, so the key skill is discriminating the root cause. A node NotReady condition often correlates with kubelet, CRI, or kernel problems; check oc describe node and inspect host logs with journalctl for kubelet or crio. Resource exhaustion shows as high C P U or memory usage; oc adm top nodes and oc describe node reveal pressure conditions and reasons for pod eviction. Networking problems show up as failed connections between pods or services; verify NetworkPolicies with oc get netpol and attempt connectivity tests with oc exec into a pod and ping or curl the target service. A common misstep is treating a connectivity failure as a routing problem when NetworkPolicies are blocking egress or ingress. When host debugging is necessary, oc debug node creates a debug pod with host access; use it cautiously because it grants privileged host inspection.

screens.title: Diagnostic toolkit: oc describe, logs, exec, debug, must-gather
screens.narratorSegment: A disciplined troubleshooting workflow reduces mean time to resolution. Begin with oc describe to read events and resource conditions; this often points to scheduling, ImagePull, or readiness issues. Next, use oc logs to read container output; add -f to follow logs in real time or -p to fetch previous container logs if a restart occurred. oc exec lets you run commands inside a container to inspect the runtime environment, check mounted volumes, or test connectivity. If the issue is host-level, oc debug node creates a privileged debug pod that gives you a host-like shell to run journalctl or inspect the filesystem — use it with caution because it grants host access. For comprehensive diagnostics, oc adm must-gather collects cluster state, logs, and artifacts into an archive that you can share with Red Hat support. A common error is skipping logs and jumping straight to node changes; logs and events usually reveal whether the fault lies in the workload or the host. Takeaway: follow a stepwise escalation: describe, logs, exec, debug node, then must-gather for full evidence collection. screens.title: Activity: Troubleshoot a failing application pod
screens.narratorSegment: This guided activity walks you through deploying a failing application and diagnosing the cause. Start by creating a project and applying a deployment that exits on startup. Watch pods with oc get pods -w until you observe CrashLoopBackOff. Then capture the pod name with a label selector and run oc describe to read events. The logs will show the application printed a message and exited; oc logs reveals the exit message and exit code. If logs are empty, oc describe often surfaces image or runtime errors. After diagnosing, you can fix the deployment by setting a healthy image and removing the failing command. This activity reinforces the core troubleshooting workflow: observe state, gather events, read logs, and change only the resource that causes the failure. A common misconception is to change many fields at once; instead, apply minimal corrective changes and re-check the pod state. Finally, once the pod stabilizes, explore Grafana for relevant metrics and Kibana for centralized logs to see how the incident is reflected across observability tools. content.html:
Code Walkthrough › Failing deployment
failing-app.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: failing-webapp
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: failing-webapp
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: failing-webapp
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: failing-container
        image: registry.access.redhat.com/ubi8/nodejs-16
        command: ["sh", "-c", "echo 'Simulating a crash...' && exit 1"]
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        resources:
          limits:
            memory: "128Mi"
            cpu: "100m"
Recovery commands
oc get pods -n troubleshooting-project
POD_NAME=$(oc get pod -l app=failing-webapp -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}' -n troubleshooting-project)
oc describe pod $POD_NAME -n troubleshooting-project
oc logs $POD_NAME -n troubleshooting-project
oc set image deployment/failing-webapp failing-container=registry.access.redhat.com/ubi8/nginx-120 -n troubleshooting-project
oc patch deployment failing-webapp --type='json' -p='[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/command"}]' -n troubleshooting-project
After patching, verify the pod becomes Running and check logs and dashboards for normal behavior.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we focus on the operational tools you need to keep an OpenShift cluster healthy. You will learn how OpenShift integrates Prometheus and Grafana for metrics and alerting, how the EFK stack centralizes application and platform logs, and how to use oc commands to diagnose and resolve common failures. We will ground each concept with short examples: exposing application metrics for Prometheus, reading container logs with oc logs, and running oc debug for node-level troubleshooting. You will also see how Fluentd collects logs and forwards them to Elasticsearch for analysis in Kibana. As an architect, your role is to combine proactive monitoring, clear alert rules, and centralized logging so incidents are detected early and investigated quickly. Throughout the lesson I will point out common mistakes, like jumping to node debugging before checking application logs or ignoring alerts from Alertmanager. By the end you will be able to read monitoring dashboards, search logs, and follow a step-by-step troubleshooting workflow that leads from symptom to root cause.

By the end of these screens you will have several verifiable competencies. First, you will be able to explain and operate OpenShift's integrated monitoring stack. That includes identifying Prometheus components such as kube-state-metrics, node-exporter, and cAdvisor, and understanding how applications expose metrics for scraping. Second, you will be able to explain the EFK logging pipeline, describe what Fluentd, Elasticsearch, and Kibana do, and why centralized logs are crucial for incident response. Each objective includes a short rationale so you understand where to apply the skill. These objectives are designed for practical use: you will perform configuration checks, query metrics, and search logs in Kibana. The skills are organized so you can both detect problems early with alerts and investigate them thoroughly with logs and diagnostic commands. Finally, a verified competency milestone accompanies each objective to help you track readiness for operational duties and support escalations.

These objectives focus on applied ability. You will practice exposing application metrics so Prometheus can scrape them, and learn the annotation pattern OpenShift expects. You will also gain the habit of checking logs first with oc logs and oc describe before assuming a node failure. Another objective is to recognize scheduling and storage symptoms, for example Pending pods due to taints or Pending PVCs due to StorageClass mismatches. Finally, you will implement best practices for alert management and log retention so your cluster remains performant. Each objective includes a quick mnemonic to help you remember the sequence: observe with metrics, verify with logs, and dig deeper with oc debug or must-gather only when necessary. These applied skills reduce wasted effort and avoid risky node-level changes when the problem lives in the workload.

Prometheus and Grafana serve complementary roles. Prometheus is a time-series metrics store and alerting engine: it scrapes endpoints, stores samples, and evaluates alerting rules. Grafana connects to Prometheus to visualize that data and turn metrics into dashboards you can use during an incident or capacity exercise. Concretely, metrics like node C P U, pod restart counts, or custom application counters are recorded as time series in Prometheus and made visible in Grafana dashboards. A common example is C P U saturation on a node: Prometheus records rising C P U usage, Alertmanager triggers an alert, and Grafana shows the trend so you can correlate spikes with deployments or scheduled jobs. A typical misconception is to treat Grafana as the data source — Grafana only queries stored metrics; it does not collect them. Another common error is relying solely on dashboards without alerting. Dashboards are great for exploration, but alerting ensures you get notified when thresholds cross. Takeaway: think of Prometheus as the collector and rule evaluator, and Grafana as the interpreter and visual surface that helps you understand the numbers.

Prometheus gathers metrics by scraping targets that expose an HTTP endpoint in a Prometheus-compatible format. OpenShift deploys several exporters that turn internal state into scraped metrics. kube-state-metrics exposes object-level data about pods, deployments, and services. node-exporter gathers host-level metrics such as C P U, memory, disk, and network statistics. cAdvisor reports container-level resource usage. Applications can also expose custom metrics and be annotated so Prometheus will scrape them. A practical example is annotating a service so Prometheus picks up a /metrics endpoint; this is often the simplest way to make application counters available. A common mistake is not exposing metrics on a stable port or forgetting the scrape annotation. Another pitfall is overwhelming Prometheus with very high-cardinality labels from application metrics. The process to ensure reliable metric collection is: verify exporter pods are healthy, confirm scrape targets in Prometheus, and test an application endpoint. Doing this prevents missing data and reduces false alerts in Alertmanager. Prometheus scrape targets and exporters means exporters and annotated services are the source of truth for prometheus metrics; verify targets and endpoints when data is missing.. In practical terms, how kube-state-metrics, node-exporter, and cadvisor feed prometheus. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

OpenShift discovers application metrics either through service discovery or explicit annotations. The recommended pattern is to annotate the Service or Pod so Prometheus will scrape a /metrics endpoint. For example, annotating a Service with prometheus. io/scrape set to true and prometheus. io/port to the correct port tells Prometheus to include that endpoint. After applying the annotation, you can verify the target in the Prometheus web UI or by checking Prometheus config in OpenShift. A practical trap is forgetting to expose the endpoint inside the container or using an ephemeral port that changes between restarts. If you don’t see metrics, check the Service and Pod labels, confirm the container serves metrics on the annotated port, and inspect Prometheus scrape targets. Misunderstanding here leads to gaps in visibility rather than broken collectors. Takeaway: a stable metrics endpoint with correct annotations ensures your application metrics are reliably collected and available for dashboards and alerting. Exposing application metrics in OpenShift means use stable annotations for prometheus scraping and validate targets to ensure application metrics appear in grafana dashboards.. In practical terms, annotate services and validate prometheus scrapes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

OpenShift's integrated logging follows the EFK pattern: Fluentd collects logs, Elasticsearch stores and indexes them, and Kibana provides a user interface for searching and visualizing logs. Fluentd runs as a DaemonSet so each node forwards container stdout/stderr, system logs, and audit logs to Elasticsearch. Elasticsearch indexes logs to make searches fast and supports aggregations for analysis. Kibana sits on top and gives you the ability to query by labels, view recent events, and build visualizations that correlate with metric alerts. A practical example: when a pod restarts repeatedly, searching Kibana for that pod name and time range often reveals stack traces or exit messages that indicate a configuration or application bug. A common mistake is not sizing or managing log retention, which can cause Elasticsearch storage exhaustion. The ClusterLogging operator controls deployment; enabling it ensures Fluentd is configured cluster-wide. Takeaway: centralized logs are essential for root cause analysis and compliance, but they require operational care — index, retention, and storage must be planned. EFK Stack — Fluentd, Elasticsearch, Kibana means efk provides a searchable, centralized store of cluster and application logs that accelerates troubleshooting and supports audits.. In practical terms, how openshift centralizes logs for troubleshooting and audit. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Fluentd is deployed as a DaemonSet so every node runs a collector that tails container logs and system journals. This node-local approach reduces cross-node log traffic and ensures logs are collected even if a pod is short-lived. Fluentd enriches logs with metadata such as namespace, pod name, and container name before forwarding them to Elasticsearch. In practice, when a pod crashes, Fluentd forwards the container output to Elasticsearch where you can search it in Kibana. A misconception is that logs are lost if a pod is short-lived; because Fluentd tails the node log files, it typically captures short-lived container output as long as Fluentd is running. Another operational concern is network reliability between Fluentd and Elasticsearch; use buffering and retries in Fluentd configuration to avoid data loss under transient network issues. Key takeaway: node-local Fluentd ensures consistent log ingestion, but the end-to-end pipeline requires attention to indexing, retention, and buffer settings. Fluentd as a DaemonSet and log flow means fluentd running on each node captures container and system logs reliably and forwards them to elasticsearch for indexing and search.. In practical terms, node-local collection and forwarding architecture. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Pod failures present with a small set of familiar symptoms. CrashLoopBackOff often means the container process exits repeatedly; the first diagnostic steps are oc describe pod to see events and oc logs to view the application output. For ImagePullBackOff, oc describe will show image pull errors — check ImageStream and registry credentials. Pending pods often indicate scheduling constraints like insufficient resources, node selectors, taints, or unresolved PVCs; oc describe pod will show scheduler messages pointing to the cause. Evicted pods usually result from node pressure, such as disk or memory exhaustion; check node status and events. A common mistake is to immediately SSH into nodes and change host settings before exhausting oc describe and oc logs; that wastes time and can introduce risk. Concrete example: a CrashLoopBackOff pod that prints "Simulating a crash" in its logs indicates the application command is exiting and requires changing the container command or image. Takeaway: start with oc describe and oc logs, interpret the events, and escalate to node-level debugging only after confirming the issue is host-related. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Node and networking issues can look similar from a pod's perspective, so the key skill is discriminating the root cause. A node NotReady condition often correlates with kubelet, CRI, or kernel problems; check oc describe node and inspect host logs with journalctl for kubelet or crio. Resource exhaustion shows as high C P U or memory usage; oc adm top nodes and oc describe node reveal pressure conditions and reasons for pod eviction. Next, use oc logs to read container output; add -f to follow logs in real time or -p to fetch previous container logs if a restart occurred. oc exec lets you run commands inside a container to inspect the runtime environment, check mounted volumes, or test connectivity. If the issue is host-level, oc debug node creates a privileged debug pod that gives you a host-like shell to run journalctl or inspect the filesystem — use it with caution because it grants host access. These concise cards capture the central observability components you will use daily. Prometheus is the time-series database and alerting system responsible for scraping exporters and evaluating rules.
